source: Topic 3, Topic 4, Fletcher (Clinical Epidemiology: The Essentials)

elements.P: Patient, Population, or Problem (characteristics, demographics, setting)
elements.I: Intervention, Exposure, or Test (treatment, diagnostic assay, prognostic factor)
elements.C: Comparison or Control (placebo, standard of care, active comparator, reference standard)
elements.O: Patient-Important Outcome (mortality, morbidity, quality of life, biomarker, adverse events)

question_types.Therapy: Assesses effect of treatment on patient outcomes (Best design: RCT)
question_types.Harm: Assesses potential toxic or adverse effects (Best design: Cohort or Case-Control)
question_types.Diagnosis: Assesses accuracy of a test vs reference standard (Best design: Cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy)
question_types.Prognosis: Assesses future health trajectory over time (Best design: Inception Cohort study)
question_types.Etiology: Investigates risk factors and disease origins (Best design: Cohort or Case-Control)

RCT.name: Randomized Controlled Trial
RCT.hierarchy_level: Highest primary study evidence for therapy
strengths: Controls both measured and unmeasured confounding

Cohort.name: Cohort Study (Prospective / Retrospective)
strengths: Direct calculation of Incidence, Cumulative Incidence, Risk Ratio (RR)
limitations: Inefficient for rare diseases with long latency

Case-Control.name: Case-Control Study
strengths: Efficient for rare diseases or long latency periods
limitations: Vulnerable to recall bias and selection bias (Berkson bias)
measures: Approximates RR under Rare Disease Assumption (< 10% or < 5%)

Cross-Sectional.name: Cross-Sectional Study (Prevalence Study)
strengths: Assesses prevalence and burden of disease

Selection_Bias.definition: Systematic differences between those selected into study and those not

Information_Bias.definition: Flaws in measuring exposure, covariate, or outcome

Confounding.definition: A third variable associated with exposure and independent cause of outcome, not in causal pathway
